chief_complaint: persistent deep bone pain in knee and palpable hard distal thigh mass in teenager
hpi_details: 16M presenting with 3-month worsening distal femur pain waking him at night, with sunburst periosteal reaction and Codman triangle on radiograph.
ideas: He thinks the hard lump and aching pain are from a deep bone bruise or bad muscle knot after getting kicked hard during soccer practice a few months ago.
concerns: He is worried that this hard lump deep in his bone could be cancer and that he might have to lose his leg and never play soccer again.
expectations: He hopes to get an MRI scan to find out what is causing the lump and receive pain medicine so he can finally sleep through the night.
social_hx: High school student, plays on the school soccer team, non-smoker

available_results.value: Aggressive metaphyseal bone-forming lesion with mixed sclerosis, sunburst periosteal reaction, and Codman triangle
available_results.note: Highly suspicious for osteosarcoma; definitive biopsy and staging remain pending.

clinical_knowledge.topic: Osteosarcoma of the distal femur evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Osteosarcoma of the distal femur is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes urgent referral to an orthopedic oncology center for staging and biopsy performed by the treating surgical team before any intervention, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: persistent deep bone pain in knee and palpable hard distal thigh mass in teenager
Key HPI features: 16M presenting with 3-month worsening distal femur pain waking him at night, with sunburst periosteal reaction and Codman triangle on radiograph.

Objective/Exam findings: Afebrile, vitals within normal limits. Firm, tender, fixed mass over the distal femoral metaphysis with overlying warmth; skin intact, no erythema. Restricted knee range of motion due to pain. Distal pulses and sensation intact. No lymphadenopathy. Labs show elevated alkaline phosphatase and LDH.
Relevant background/PMH: No significant past medical history
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Osteosarcoma of the distal femur.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Ewing sarcoma without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Night pain waking from sleep.
management_principles: Urgent referral to an orthopedic oncology center; the diagnostic biopsy must be performed by the treating surgical team to avoid compromising future limb-salvage options
Staging workup: MRI of the entire affected bone to assess local extent and skip lesions, CT chest for pulmonary metastases, bone scan or PET-CT, and baseline LDH/alkaline phosphatase
Neoadjuvant chemotherapy (e.g., methotrexate, doxorubicin, cisplatin) followed by limb-salvage resection or amputation depending on tumor response and anatomic extent
Provide the patient and family with psychosocial support and counseling given the diagnosis and prolonged multidisciplinary treatment course.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

must_ask.say: Does the pain wake you up at night, separate from activity?
Have you or your parents noticed a hard lump near your knee?
Have you had any unexplained weight loss, fevers, or fatigue?
Was there any injury to the leg before this started?

must_ask.objective: Explain the need for urgent oncology workup
must_ask.say: These findings need urgent assessment by a bone-tumor specialist team. They will arrange the imaging and, if needed, plan a biopsy so it does not compromise treatment.

history.answer: My right knee and lower thigh have been aching constantly for months, and lately the deep ache wakes me up at night.
It is only in my right lower thigh right above the knee; my left leg and all other joints feel completely fine.
It started gradually about three months ago and has steadily grown worse over time.
It feels like a deep, gnawing bone ache that usually sits around a six or seven out of ten.
There is a hard lump right above my knee that feels slightly warm to touch, but the skin is not red.
I do not have stiffness when I wake up in the morning, just the same persistent deep ache.
Running on the soccer field definitely makes it hurt worse, but resting on the couch does not make it go away.
I can put weight on it, but I walk with a limp and bending the knee completely or climbing stairs hurts a lot.
I play soccer, but I never had a bad tackle, heard a pop, or felt my knee lock or give out.
No, I have never experienced any knee pain or joint swelling before this started.
No, I haven't had any fever, chills, or night sweats.
I feel normal energy during the day, and my weight has been steady.
No rashes, no mouth sores, and no red or painful eyes.
I have no lower back stiffness in the morning and no pain in my heels or toes.
No, I haven't had any diarrhea, pain when urinating, or recent sore throats.
I don't drink alcohol, eat regular school meals, and don't take water pills.
I have never received any joint shots, taken steroids, or had surgery on my legs.
I have never had sex or been sexually active.
It wakes me up around two or three in the morning with a deep throbbing ache that makes it hard to fall back asleep.
About a month ago I felt a hard, immovable bump right above my right knee on the inner side of my thigh.
I figured I just got kicked really hard during soccer practice a few months back and ended up with a nasty deep bone bruise that won't heal.
It hurts so bad at night that I can't sleep, and I'm really terrified that this lump might be a bone tumor and they'll have to amputate my leg.
I just want an MRI to tell me what this bump actually is, and something strong for the pain so I can finally get a full night's sleep.
I have always been healthy and have never been diagnosed with any chronic medical illnesses.
I have never had an operation and have never stayed in a hospital overnight.
I don't take any regular prescriptions, only an occasional ibuprofen that barely takes the edge off.
I don't have any allergies to medications, foods, or anything else.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used vape pens.
I do not drink any alcohol.
I am a high school sophomore living with my parents, and I play on the school soccer team.
There is no history of bone tumors, childhood cancers, or early serious illnesses in my family.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 118/76 mmHg, heart rate 72 beats/min, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, temperature 36.8°C, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Alert, well-developed adolescent male sitting on the exam table in no acute cardiopulmonary distress, appearing mildly anxious.
Firm, tender, fixed mass over the right distal femoral metaphysis with mild overlying warmth, intact skin without erythema, and right knee flexion restricted to 90 degrees due to pain.
Antalgic gait favoring the right lower extremity, with shortened stance phase and reluctance to bear full weight on the right leg.
Right dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are 2+ and symmetric bilaterally with capillary refill under 2 seconds.
Light touch and pinprick sensation are intact and symmetric throughout both lower extremities.
Strength is 5/5 in bilateral hips, ankles, and toes, while active right knee flexion and extension are limited by local pain.
Skin over both lower extremities is intact without erythema, rashes, ecchymoses, or draining sinuses.
No cervical, supraclavicular, or axillary lymphadenopathy palpable.
No inguinal lymphadenopathy or femoral hernia palpable bilaterally.
